blocks.x: I'll make a note that we're interviewing Mrs. Adams and the date is April the 18th, 1962 and we're over at her home on 1560 North Johnson. Do you mind giving your full name?
My full name is Dolly Marie Adams.
And what was your name before you were married? Dolly DeRux. DeRux. So you were a daughter of one of Professor Mineta's sisters.
That's right. My mother, which is Professor Mineta's sister, she was also a musician.
Yes, I remember that very well.
She played the piano, violin, trumpet, and my daddy, he was a well-known trumpet player.
Yes, Professor Mineta told us a little bit about him, but not so much, no doubt you can tell us more about him. That was Lewis DeRux. Lewis was his name.
Yeah. He played in the old Eureka and Excelsa bands.
When did he die? Do you remember the date about?
He died October 1st. Just a minute. This is 58. It's 12 years ago.
12 years ago.
Do you remember about how old he was? He was 74.
74 then. I never did get to know him. I came down off and on for vacations in New Orleans. I was from up north at that time. So I never did get to know him.
Well, he retired a little earlier than most musicians do.
So he didn't play in late years then?
No, he didn't play. After he got about 50 years old, he retired from it.
His main instrument was the carnet or trumpet? Trumpet.
Carnet in those days. Yes. In those days.
Do you mind telling when you were born? Some ladies don't like to tell their age.
Well.
It's not necessary if you don't like to.
Going back to Dixieland Music, I have to tell the truth. I was born January 11th, 1904. Oh, yeah.
Can you tell us when you first started in music and the very first music you remember hearing?
Well, I first started playing at 7 years old. And my first numbers on the piano were Casey Jones and Steamboat Bill.
I know the Casey Jones. I don't know the Steamboat Bill. I don't think so.

Well, that was my very first numbers. I had listened at it for a long time and was just wishing for the time I'd get a piano. And I had it in my mind so much that when I got a piano, I just went right and played it. I pictured the notes in my mind so that I could go right and play it. You just played it at the key. That's right.
Was your father playing music then that you can remember?
Oh, yes, yes, yes. I played with him.
Played with him. Who was your first teacher? Did he help you or did you go to someone else?
No, my father didn't help me. Professor Mineta taught me my first lessons. And then when I was in high school at St. Mary's Academy, I took some of the lessons from then.
Did your mother still play at that time?
Yes, she played until she died. She did all the time? She died New Year's Day. Yes, I remember.
I went to the funeral.
That's right. She played piano the night before she died.
She did that late. I didn't know if she kept the...

That's right. Yes, you were at the funeral. I remember that. Well, that, the New Year's Eve night, there was a party at my sister's house and she played the piano. She played that late. She played insane.
That's remarkable. Yes. Did she ever help you much with the piano in your home? No doubt she was... Well, I didn't need help

because I was so interested and enthused all I needed for her was to buy a piano. That was all. And I went right to work on it. And when I was nine years old, my brother, he was a violinist. And I went out and played parties at nine years old with my brother. That's right. Nine years old. I was playing parties. And then when I was 13 is when I started out with Professor Mineta. I started playing in his band. Yes.
Can you remember who else was in the band at that time? And what did they have in the band?

Well, at that time, they had... Each night that they played, it seemed they had different musicians, different jobs. I know how the band was. A lot of times it was that way. Sometimes it was Louis Armstrong.
Did he have a regular name for the band? Or just...
Oh, I can think of it.
It seems he always was he had a special name. I can't think of it.

Well, he may know what he called it, but we always called it Mineta's Band. Mineta's Band. Yeah. Well, at times, Louis Armstrong played with us. Then other times, there was Kid Ory. It was... Is that a fellow? I can't think of him right now, but I will get to it.
What instrument?
Trumpet. Trumpet. He died.
It was Joe Oliver.
I played with Joe Oliver. Yeah.
Did you work with him?
Joe Oliver. That's right.
Later called him King Oliver.
That's right. King Oliver and Kid Howard.
Oh, yeah. That's Kid Howard. He's a kid. He's still playing right now.

I played with them at that time. And, oh, I like Bigard. Oh, yes. Yeah. And the drummer, the drummer. That's right. And there was a Raymond Dugall. Now, I don't know if he's living or dead. No, I don't know. Never know. He was in those times. Well, I played with him, too. Raymond... Dugall.
How was the name spelled? Are those French names? No, it was a French name.
I would not spell it. I don't know him. I don't know him. I would really know him. He played trumpet, too? He played drums. Oh, drums. That's right.
No, I don't know him.
And then, when I was, oh, about 15, I started with the Creole Serenaders.
Oh, was that with Peter Bocas? Bocas.
I played a long time with them. Oh, yeah. And then, I had my own band for a while playing at the Othello Theater on Rampart Street. Oh. How far up?
Where was that? I don't remember.
That was in the third block.
Third block? Of Rampart. Oh, uptown. Uptown.
Yeah. They had a theater there, the Othello Theater. Yes, I don't know. That's before my time. And I had my own band there.
Was that for movies, or did they have vaudeville and shows?
They had vaudeville and pictures at the time.
How big a band did they use about?
Well, they used only four pieces. Four pieces. Yeah. And those four pieces was T-Boy Dominic on a trumpet. I think he's still living.
I think he's in California. He used to be in the Eureka Band when I first came here.
Then there's Joe Welsh on the violin. Well, he is dead.
Yes, I never knew him.
And the drummer, we only know him by Kid Faso.
Oh, yes. I have pictures of him yet.
You have? Well, that was the drummer in that band and myself. Well, that was my band.
Yes.
I was just about 16 then. 16. And then after I quit with Menev, that is after he retired from playing. He retired to teach.
He doesn't teach you. I think it's in the 20s. That's right. It's the early 20s, I think.
Then I started out with my brothers, Oivin and Longin. And Lawrence threw it. Oivin was a great trombonist. Lawrence was a trumpet, very good trumpet player and music arranger.
So you've always been in family bands most of the time. That's right. Still have you.

And I played for years with them until Oivin died. And Lawrence became very ill. Then I had to look for another way. Then this one here, that's my oldest boy. He was just fresh in from the Army. And Gerald was then 16 and Placif was 14. That's the two boys you've seen at the preservation hall. Well, we started out a trio there. And we've been together. Well, I said a trio. We first started the trio because Placif was in the Army. And when he came back, it was four pieces. And then we went along there.

Well, I think of it. I wonder if there's anything else you could tell us about your father. Since, as I say, we never did get much information about the different bands. You say he played the Eureka. Did he play mostly brass bands or did he play in dance orchestras too?
He played in dance orchestras and brass bands. And brass bands too. Parade bands and all those.
Now, do you remember where he started? Who was his teacher?
Well, that I wouldn't know.

Because I know some of Professor Mineta's uncle even, Norm, he always speaks of him as his uncle, Norm, that played trumpet way back even... Well, that probably was his teacher. Might have been his teacher in Boston.
Yeah.
Probably.
Probably was his teacher.

You didn't hear him talk about him much? Well, no. He played a little short E-flat. Norm and Mineta played a little short E-flat trumpet, I think, in the brass bands, mostly brass bands. Did he ever play much in Algiers? Had their family been raised in Algiers too? Your father's family?
They were born and raised in Algiers. Those were there. Uh-huh.
I know that.
And he practically played all those barades and funerals and all such as that.
Do you remember if you ever played in Henry Allen's band? There's a young Henry Allen they call Red Allen now, but the old man that was also named Henry Allen... I think so.
...had a brass band that pushed famous over there. Because he played at all those bands. All of the different bands. Yeah. All those bands in that time. All those brass bands.
Do you remember any particular dance band groups that he might have worked with?
Well, I can only remember... One, he was a bass player. He was Charlie DeBurgis.
Oh, yes. Professor Mineta studied, took lessons from him. He did? He must have taught and played different instruments. He most had it.
When he was a boy... I do remember hearing my daddy play, say that Charlie DeBurgis played with them.
And played bass.
Yeah. They went all over little country places and played as far as Baton Rouge and all over, you know. Professor Mineta told us... He played dance music. Well, that was called the string dance.
He said he came down here from Arkansas or someplace up that way and was first playing guitar. He even played harmonica and different instruments of that kind.
He was a very good musician. Very good.

And I came across a piece that he wrote, I didn't get the entire piece, I think just the first page in the cover, called Algiers Girl. Just last year I found it. Mm-hmm. In the volunteers. And a lot of old sheet music I was going through. Professor Mineta had never seen it either.
He didn't know it was published. He hadn't seen it either. Well, I declare it.
So he had some music published at least then. And that was... Mr. DeBurgis then played with your father.
Yes, he did.
If you want to stop and answer the phone anytime, it's all right.
Is your dad in the bag?
So... Can you think of any other bands or musicians you might have worked with?
Well, that was about covered, playing with all the brass bands around here.
Yes, I put it. I meant in the dance band field or anything.
Well, I can only remember Charlie DeBurgis. You see, that was a little before my time. I mean, I was too young to even have an interest in it, you see.
Did your father work in music full-time or did he have another trade?
Oh, no, he was a butcher. He was a butcher. Yeah. He was a butcher.
Most of the musicians worked that as a sideline a lot of times just on weekends.
Yeah, well, he was a butcher all these lines. And that gave him time for...
Just worked at night then occasionally.
Yeah, he had a lot of time then for the braids and all of that, you know, because he was finished at 12 o'clock. The markets used to close then at 12 o'clock.
Oh, that's right. They opened up real early. I've heard how the French market did that way.
They were regular markets. There was nothing else sold in them but meat. Just meat. And they would close at 12, so that would give him time.
Can you say he retired from music then? What do you remember?
Anything you remember that I don't?
I don't know.
Huh?
I was going to tell you my time I'm a father that you forgot.
Which one?
The grandpa player.
That's what I'm trying to remember?
Big I, Lloyd. The bass player.
Big I, Lloyd. Yeah.
Boy, yeah. That part of that to you whether it was Crossford River going to a job or a bias of when he turned the skiff over and everything.
You see, there's a lot of things that skips my memory, you know? Big I, Lloyd. He's got a good memory. He can refresh my memory.
Chris, uh... Chris Kelly, probably. Chris Kelly. Chris Kelly. They worked together. Grandpa often told us about those guys.
I knew Big I, Lloyd. I made some records of him once before he died in 1949. A couple weeks after I was part of this band once and issued some of the records.
You see, uh... My dad used to relate a lot of things to the kids, you know? And they have a better memory than I have.
Well, sometimes it's that way. I know my memory isn't very good anymore. It used to be good, but not now.
Well, after you get to that age, you know, your memory began to lax on you.

So that's interesting. You work with, uh... They call him Louis DeLeo is his real name, but everybody called him Louis Nelson. His name really wasn't... His father's name wasn't Nelson, but I think his father once had worked for some people for the name of Nelson. Somehow that name got started. And then they called him Big I. He didn't like that nickname, but his Louis DeLeo was his real name. Oh, yeah. He lived right here in the neighborhood not far down on the Durban Street near St. Bernard Circle.
Well, um... You say he's dead.

He's dead. Died in 1949. Oh, I see. He's one of the most famous clarinets. Professor Renetta talks a lot about him. He was a close friend of his. He worked a lot with him too. So he retired when he was about 50 or so he said from music then.
Yes, about that.

He retired. And he lived to be 72 or 74? 74. 74, then. That's a good age. He lived to that age. Did your mother ever, I've never talked to Professor Manetta much about his sisters, but did your mother ever play any professional? I didn't think she did. No, she never worked professionally. I didn't think she did. No, she only played at home. She played at home. And never did give up the music then?
No, no, no, never did. It has come down the line. I am now with the third generation.
Yes, that's right.
Then I have a grandson that's playing drums, and I hope to be with him. He's nine years old.
It's nine years.
But I hope to live long enough to make that fourth generation.
It would be nice, wouldn't it? Yeah. Only if he lives in, I mean, if you all keep playing, another five or six years, you'll be ready.
I'm sure you'll be.
I'm sure you will. They don't start as young, though, now as they used to, Harley. Do they?
Well, this kid started since he was two years old.

Oh, really? I mean, going out to play music like they did in the old days. Well, there's some laws against it now. I guess there is. Like you said, you were playing in dance bands when you were 16 or so. Oh, 13 I started in dance bands. 13, yeah. 13. 13. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. So Harley would see a girl doing that now. Okay.

Well, I was just a great big girl, you know. And if you just look at me, you would never say I was 13. Yeah. So I could pass that way, you see. A lot of children. I could never question my age. Yeah. But nevertheless, I was 13 years old.

Can you remember anything about your lessons with Professor Renetta? Did he, what books or anything else he might have used or how he taught you? So I see I've gone to some of his lessons on the clarinet and also a friend of mine that took a few piano lessons once, a boy from Chicago. And do I know something about his teaching? I just wondered in those days back then.
I only used the James Belloc.
James, I'm not even familiar with that.
James Belloc.
It was a regular method book?
A regular method, a beginner.
Yes.
And then after I went to St. Maher's Academy, well, I had to take music with them.
Yes.
You see, I took music with them.

I know today Professor Renetta doesn't teach much in the line of jazz or improvising and, you know, just playing popular tunes. He sticks mostly to the more classical music and their methods. Yes, he did. Did he do that when you were studying with him too or did he ever help you with some of the late tunes?
Oh, no. Well, you see, I didn't need any help on the plane.
You were able to pick those right up anyway.
Yeah. I just took lessons to learn to read. To read, no. But I didn't need any help at all on the plane because I started out in the jazz time.
Yes.
And when I played with my brothers, well, it was swing time.
A lot of times in the old days, about that time, they were calling it rag time too, weren't they?
Well, rag time too, yeah.
Do you remember any of the old rags, like the Joplin rags and all? Professor Renetta still played some of those. I was the old playing ball.
I don't remember. We played some of them.
Well, like Panama always. Yes, Panama. Of course, they used the other night.
Red Rose Ray. Oh, yes. Sensation is plenty. Oh, yes. All those old days. Yes. Oh, we play all that. Still good numbers, actually. Oh, wonderful. They're wonderful numbers.
I enjoyed hearing your band the other night.

Most of them is three-part rags. And now I came back. Let's get back to the time of music. I played the Dixieland, the rake time, the swing with my brothers. And then after we got to the boys, well, I had to go in a more modern direction.
Yes, of course. Music keeps changing like everything else.
Then I had to change to modern. So we all, me and the outfit, we are versatile. We play every type of music. I taught the boys the Dixieland music, you see.
Did you teach them most of their music, too, on the different instruments?
Well, I only had to teach them the fundamentals of music.
Yes, and the reading and the time.

They picked it up right now. And Justin took lessons from Professor Mineta, for the guitar. Where is it? The guitar. The drummer, Pussy. He just picked it up. Didn't have to teach them. No more than the fundamentals. Yes.
There's a lot of children that way, especially here in New Orleans, where they've heard all of this music all their life and have that background. A lot of them do it with very, very special.
Gerald bought a bass on a Wednesday and played his first job on Thursday. Oh, really?
And he played a little bit on the piano or anything else?
I guess he knew a little bit about music. He used to play a little bit on the piano.
He knew a little music already.
And he just worked all night with the bass. All day and all night. And all the next day until it was time for the job. And he played the job.
Did he get to rehearse with him before in the band? No, no, no. Just went right on to play?
No, he just went right to it.
How old was he when he did that? Sixteen. Sixteen? Mm-hmm. Very good.
And Gerald is still a very good piano player, too. Mm-hmm.
You still practice on the instrument or you just wait until you work someplace?
No, we don't all. We don't ever practice.
You don't? No. No. No.
Justin, this is the oldest one. That's a guitar player. He plays along with, around with, right now he's playing with a modern band, you know, a rock and roll band, but he's played with Dixon.

Well, it's certainly the same type of music in some ways, as long as you know the chords. That's it. So you can play any of them. Are there any other bands or other jobs that you can think of, like you mentioned, like after that movie job? How long were you there? Or the theater job? That was with vaudeville, too.
Vaudeville. I must have been there about a year.
Did they have any other acts, like famous singers or artists that would come in from our town, if you can remember at that time?
I can remember some. I remember Dad James. I don't know if you can think about him. I don't remember. He was a good singer. And Luke Cannon.

We collect records. Of course, I've always collected records for 20 or 30 years now. And I have a lot of the old time records, too. The period of Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey and everyone of that kind. Oh, yes. So unless a person recorded, I wouldn't know a lot of those names.
Well, now, I wouldn't really know if they recorded those things or not. But they were in, they were standards. They stayed at the show. Other acts came, but they stayed.
You had to play for the silent movies?
Yeah, I played for both. I played for the silent movies.
Did the whole orchestra play? No, no, no.
Just the piano.
Just the piano. That's where they used to be when I drove. Just the piano.
And then, I think they had four of Baudrill's Day.
Which side of the street? Is that the lake or riverside? I don't remember.
It's on the lakeside.
Is that about, is that very near the Astoria Hotel?
It could be somewhere around there. I just remember some third black. I think it was destroyed.

Must have been torn down. Pelican was in there, too, and the restaurant, the famous restaurant. They had music there, too. Yeah. For a long time. But that whole part of town is going now since they had the new... It is, it is, yeah. The Civic Center and all the city hall and everything along in there. Is there anything else about your life that, uh, music and the musicians that you heard and played with that you could add? For instance, were there any other outstanding pianists? Everyone knows Professor Minette, of course, is a great pianist. But were there any others that you remember hearing and watching when you were young and learning?
Well, they didn't have very many piano plays at that time. I do remember Walter Deku.

Oh, yes. He's still living, too. We've never interviewed him. Yeah. He's hard to find. He doesn't play anymore. He gave up music. He had some mental trouble, too, I think, you know, for a while, too. Oh, I see.
But he was popular at the time that I was popular.
I heard he play, too. He made some records with the Bunk Johnson, the trumpet, the famous trumpet player who he knew quite well. He's dead now, too. Any other pianists that you heard?
I guess I heard a gang of them,
but I tried to remember. It's hard to remember all those. I tried to remember. Did you get out much? I know a lot of times girls don't get out much, you know, to go around to hear music like Boa.
Well, I got out because I was with my uncle.
Because of the freshman effort?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah.
That's why I always had someone with me. Yes. See, when I left my uncle, I went with my brothers, and they were with my sons.
Yeah. You've always been there.

So I've always been well chaperoned. Yeah. And at the time, though, that Emanuel was very popular with the piano, too. And he played the clarinet to give me a chance at the piano, you see. Oh, yeah. Yeah.

You know, he could play all the instruments, and he still does, too. Yeah, he does. Like the other one, there's two instruments at once. I wondered about his piano playing. I've only heard him, of course, the last six or seven years, really, a little longer, maybe. And I never did hear him like about 30 years ago when he used to play all the time. Did he play a much different style? Yes, yes.
He played the styles that had them.
Because he still gets around awfully well on the piano, doesn't he?
He has remarkable. I must say, not to brag about it, but he was the best New Orleans. That's what people have told. Really the best there was in New Orleans.
Because even today, he plays remarkably well. Yes, he do. He plays almost more piano than anyone you hear nowadays. When he gets going, good.
Did you hear him at the presentation hall?
Yes. Yes, very well.
I think he done real well with him.

And with his two instruments, I've heard him on guitar, too. I've heard him play those two pieces. He plays Dixie like he did on the piano, with Dixie in one hand and Yankee Doodle and the other. He does that on guitar, too. He mixes up the two tunes and keeps them going with the two fingers. And the Cardian, I've heard him play on that, too, very well.
Yeah, he play about every instrument. Yes, about everything. I never saw him play a bass. That's about the only one. No, that's right.
I never did either. No, I never did.

You see, bass tears up his fingers so much. You know, he gets such terrible cones. Yes. And he likes to preserve his fingers, too, you know. So I guess that's why he never bothered too much with the bass. But he could play it.
Well, I bet he could, too. Yeah, yeah. Bass horn and all.
Yes.
Can you think of anything else you'd like to add? There's another minute or so on here.
Can you think of something, Justin? You've got a better memory than me, even though you're younger.
Tell them all the old guys that you played.
All I could think of, I think of maybe tonight. Oh, yes.
I suppose you're right. You said the bands in those days, they all played, were different each week and you played with just almost everybody in town. Or Papai Teo, the Renzetio. Oh, yeah.
Yeah, I played
with him, too.
Yeah, I played with him, too. Or Piku. The Renzetio.
Piku, I guess, too.
See, at the time, yeah, all that. When we played with the Creole Serenators, Oh, yes. The Peter Bocas. The father was Paul. Had Peter, Henry, and Charlie, three sons, and their brother-in-law, Teo.
That was L'Renzetio. Yes, L'Renzetio. Married their sister, I know. Yeah.
That's what their outfit consists of.
I never did get to hear of L'Renzetio, but he made some records.
Oh, he was the best.
He has a brother still living here, too.
He was the very best you ever heard.
What are you doing? How you doing?
This is my husband,

Mr. Lissett. What are you doing in there, Mr. Adams? Mr. Adams. I was talking about the old, look at that beautiful little rabbit. Looks pretty tame. We're just about two. I'm not interrupting. No, no, no. We're just about two here, I guess, unless there's something else you can add.
Well, is anything interesting that you would like for me to add?

Well, I'm not thinking mostly about any of the musicians, any other musicians you can think of that you might have played with. For instance, the Creole Serenaders, you might add another word about that or so. Where did they play and what kind of jobs did they have? Dance, parties,
house parties.
At one time, I know some of the group had played with Pierron, like out at Spanish Fort. Did they ever have any long engagement anyplace, like any special club?
Well, that was a different outfit at the time. That was with Peter. Yeah. Peter played in that part. But that wasn't the rest. The Creole Serenaders consisted of his brothers.

Yes. Forgive me for a second. I just want to... Sure, sir. Yeah, perfect. Thank you. I'm sorry. I don't want to be back. Get around. I'll be back. I'll be back. I'll be back. Okay. Mostly, like parties and club dates, things of that kind.
Oh, yeah. There's things like that. Now, can you think of anything else, Justin? That's my counselor.
How long did you work with the Creole Serenaders?
Oh, I worked with them for years. I got married and left them. I went away when I got married. Well, I might add...
What date was that when you got married? I guess most people remember when they got married.
Well, I remember even though I tried to forget.
I'm not trying to embarrass you.
I think it was in 22.
Yeah, I think that's when it was. 22.
Before that, then you...
with the ceremony.
Yeah, and it took 15 years out to raise a family
and then went right back to me.
And I've been waking ever since.
I'm glad I got to hear you the other night and even if it was only a short time, I was over there a couple of sets.
Oh, you didn't stay very long?

Well, we stayed a couple of sets there. The last set we were there and then the other one the first time, right before Professor Mineta played. He played, we missed one of his appearances too. He played twice, he said.
The first one was the best.
Yes, I know he played all of his instruments and played a couple of numbers on the piano then too.
It was really good, the first one.
We enjoyed your band a lot too.
Well, I'm glad you did.
So I think that if that covers, unless you have anything else you want to add, but it just stays just about off.
Well, you'll have to do like you do with Mineta.
Come back again if we get to work. Come back again if I think of somebody else. That's a more questions.
Yeah.
stuff
